brief.h: Hormuz: first two-sided movement since the accord collapsed
brief.t: Washington put a concrete offer on the table through Pakistan's General Munir — sanctions relief plus lifting the naval blockade in exchange for reopening and a halt to proxy attacks — while Iran and Oman agreed a temporary corridor with a mine-clearance project and technical talks on a permanent one. Tehran says it will respond soon, but also repeated that the strait is not open until the US honours the June memorandum. That is the fifth near-breakthrough followed by a restated condition.

brief.h: Moscow rejects the heart of the joint Western plan
brief.t: Peskov dismissed the Donbas free-economic-zone component of the August 23 text outright, after Putin called the intermediary proposals 'exotic.' The one thing that made the plan new — a single agreed Western text — has now been answered, negatively. The front is unchanged: 203 engagements in a day, Pokrovsk heaviest.

brief.h: Summit choreography continues under sanctions fire
brief.t: A day after Economic D-Day sanctioned Chinese entities, both capitals are still publicly preparing a 'very positive' Xi visit for September 24, with Rubio and Wang Yi working the agenda. Leverage being stacked, not a rupture — exactly what the hypothesis lab predicts.

lesson: Denmark charged every ship entering the Baltic a toll at Elsinore castle for 428 years — the Sound Dues, 1429 to 1857. It worked while Denmark was strong and the fee bearable; it ended when the rising maritime powers simply bought the strait's freedom out in a lump-sum treaty. Iran's permit authority is trying to be Denmark. Its enforcement — boarding, seizing, shooting — keeps veering toward Egypt's 1967 closure of the Straits of Tiran instead, which the world treated as an act of war within three weeks. Which precedent wins is, more or less, the whole Hormuz forecast.

lecture.title: The Toll Collector, the Prince, and the End of the Interlude

sections.t: Iran's permit regime feels unprecedented; it isn't. Denmark ran the Sound Dues from 1429 to 1857 — every ship entering the Baltic paid the crown at Elsinore, financing the Danish state for four centuries, until the maritime nations bought the strait free by treaty. The double lesson: a chokepoint toll is durable when the collector is strong and the fee bearable, fatal when the collector is weak and patience runs out. Nasser survived nationalizing Suez in 1956 because the superpowers split; Egypt closed Tiran in 1967 and had war inside three weeks. Iran's PGSA is trying to be Denmark; its kinetic enforcement keeps veering toward Tiran. And today's US convoy escorts rerun Operation Earnest Will (1987–8), which ended with the US Navy destroying half of Iran's fleet in a day after a single mine strike. Both governments know this history — which is why the standoff is so combustible.

The Islamic Republic's founding claim — guardianship of the jurist — was a rejection of dynasty; 1979 overthrew a hereditary monarch. Mojtaba's eight-day accession, over his father's written objection to family succession and under documented Revolutionary Guard pressure, quietly converted the republic into the thing it was born to destroy: a monarchy guarded by praetorians. Praetorian institutions — Rome's Guard, the Ottoman Janissaries, Pakistan's army economy — convert national crisis into institutional power; the emergency is the business model. An IRGC collecting two-million-dollar tolls in bitcoin while the national export terminal sits idle is not irrational. It is the type behaving as the type always has. That is why a managed, toll-preserving reopening is far likelier than a free strait: institutions do not dissolve themselves.

Russia has no natural western frontier — the North European Plain runs flat from the Urals to the Atlantic — and every Russian state since Muscovy has answered that geography by pushing the buffer outward. This is the latest partition war over the borderlands, settled into attrition, and attrition wars end through exhaustion, usually via armistice: Korea 1953 is the governing template. The obstacle is the credible-commitment problem, and Ukraine is its textbook victim — in 1994 it surrendered the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal for the Budapest Memorandum's paper assurances, from, among others, Russia. Every guarantee now on offer is negotiated in the shadow of that betrayal.

Beijing's current quiet should be read through 1914, not 1938. The dangerous moments come from window logic — Germany went to war partly because its generals believed Russia would be unbeatable by 1917. China's demographics have peaked and US munitions are visibly depleted; a closing-window calculation could form within a decade. Against it: nuclear deterrence, the hardest amphibious operation in warfare, and fabs worth more unburnt. The coast-guard creep east of Taiwan is Schelling's salami tactics — each slice too thin to fight over. Gray-zone strategies fail only when they force the defender to a bright line; whether the slicing continues through the September summit is this month's test of which game Beijing is playing.

What you are watching is the closing of the unipolar interlude — the thirty years when one navy underwrote every strait and major-power war was priced near zero. It is ending the way Britain's underwriting ended between 1914 and 1947: piecemeal, strait by strait, with the old hegemon monetizing what it once provided free — note Washington now charging for convoy protection — and middle powers suddenly indispensable: Pakistan mediating, Oman hosting, the Gulf selling to both blocs. The nineteenth century would recognize this world instantly. The twentieth would not.

Four structural calls. This is probably the last great oil-chokepoint crisis — 2026 is doing to electrification what 1973 did to the IEA and North Sea oil; by the 2040s Hormuz matters like coaling stations did in 1950 (moderate-high confidence). The proliferation dam is cracked: Ukraine disarmed and was invaded, Iran lacked the bomb and was decapitated, North Korea is untouched — expect one to three new nuclear or threshold states in twenty years, the worst trend on the board (moderate). Russia's trajectory is Ottoman: declining, dangerous because declining, ending as junior partner to the neighbor it once dominated (high confidence on direction, none on timing). And the hinge of the century is whether a democracy keeps paying hegemony's domestic costs — decided less in Taiwan than in Washington's budgets and gas prices (genuinely uncertain). Reading: Kennedy's Rise and Fall of the Great Powers; Schelling's Arms and Influence; Yergin's The Prize; Kotkin on Russia.
